vignette:
Mara is a 63-year-old sculptor who has been married for thirty-seven years. She came to therapy at her husband’s urging, though she herself is uncertain what talking could possibly change. The event that fractured her life happened four years ago, in the late afternoon, in her own studio—a converted garage behind their home in a quiet suburban neighborhood. A man she had hired to help with heavy lifting for a public art commission arrived early, and before she could even set down her chisel, he had pinned her against the workbench, his hand over her mouth. She remembers the smell of turpentine and the way the concrete floor felt cold against her back. She did not scream. She told herself afterward that she had frozen because it was the safest thing to do, but that thought has never brought her any peace.

In the months that followed, Mara found herself unable to step into her studio. She told her husband she needed a break, that her hands were tired, that she had lost her inspiration. But what she could not say was that every time she passed the door, she saw the chisel on the floor where it had fallen, and she felt again the weight of his body and the shame of her own stillness. She had always believed herself to be a woman of conviction, someone who would fight, who would not be made a victim. Now she could not reconcile that woman with the one who had lain there, compliant, bargaining silently for it to be over. She came to believe that she had acted in ways that went against everything she was—that she had betrayed her own values in that moment of surrender—and this thought hollowed her out. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore. She stopped answering calls from the gallery that represented her, and she let the commission deadline pass without explanation.

Mara began to feel safe only in her bedroom, with the door locked and the blinds drawn. She would sit for hours on the edge of the bed, her hands folded in her lap, listening. The sound of a siren from the street—even a distant one—would send her heart racing, because it reminded her of the police she had not called, of the report she had never filed. She had told herself there was no point: the man was a subcontractor, no one would believe her, and the institution she might have turned to had already failed her in ways she could not articulate. The sirens became a kind of accusation. When her husband moved too quickly through the room, reaching for a book or turning toward her unexpectedly, she would flinch, her body bracing as if for impact. She could not explain it to him without sounding afraid of him, which she was not. But the fear had its own logic: if she had been caught off guard once, she could be caught off guard again, and her vigilance was the only thing keeping her alive.

The more she stayed in her room, the more the negative appraisals grew. She would think about her inaction and feel a wave of shame so strong it made her nauseous, and that shame would confirm for her that she was not safe anywhere except in this small, locked space. And the smaller her world became, the more vulnerable she felt to any reminder of what had happened. Her youngest son came to visit for Thanksgiving, and she could barely look at him, because he had the same build as the man, and the resemblance made her stomach turn. She knew this was irrational, but knowing did not stop the reaction. She began to avoid him, making excuses not to answer his calls, and after a few months he stopped calling as often. Mara told herself this was for the best.

What finally brought her to seek help was not her own suffering but her husband’s quiet despair. He had found her one afternoon sitting on the bathroom floor, the water running, staring at nothing. He asked her if she wanted to die, and she said no, but she was not sure she meant it. She agreed to come to therapy because she could see that her staying alive was now something she owed to someone else. What frightens her most is not the memory itself but the possibility that talking about it will make it more real, and that she will have to face the woman she became on that concrete floor. She hopes, though she cannot say it aloud, that somewhere in this process she might find a version of herself that is not defined by that single, frozen moment.
